title: Arp 143
caption: Interacting galaxies Arp 143, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Arp 143 · constellation Lynx · about About 191 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, Julianne Dalcanton (Center for Computational Astrophysics, Flatiron Inst. / UWashington)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: On the right, a distorted spiral galaxy glitters with a triangle of new stars, and on the left sits a plainer companion. The pair is Arp 143, about 191 million light-years away in Lynx. The busy one is NGC 2445, and its partner is NGC 2444.

Astronomers suggest the two galaxies passed through each other in a head-on collision, setting off a burst of star birth in gas-rich NGC 2445, where thousands of stars are forming. Head-on collisions can make rings of new stars, but here NGC 2444 still holds its partner in a gravitational grip, pulling away gas and bending the ring into a triangle.

NGC 2444 has also drawn out streamers of young, blue stars that seem to form a bridge between the two galaxies. They appear to be among the first in a wave of star formation that moved inward. Researchers estimate these stars formed some 50 million to 100 million years ago, while nearer the center of NGC 2445 the newest stars are just 1 million to 2 million years old.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F475W in blue, F606W in green, and F814W and F665N in red.
understand.eye: The colors are hues assigned to several filters, including the narrow F665N, and Hubble's sharpness picks out some individual stars in NGC 2445, the brightest and most massive in the galaxy.

explore: Most of the bright blue clumps are groups of stars, while the pink blobs are huge, young clusters still wrapped in dust and gas. NGC 2444 has been stretched into an odd shape too. It holds only old stars and makes no new ones, because it lost its gas long before this encounter.
